svg.title: Mitochondrion: regions and what happens in each
svg.desc: A schematic mitochondrion: a rounded double boundary, an outer and an inner membrane, with the inner one folded back and forth into cristae. The folding is the point, because it gives the inner membrane far more area than the outer one, and that membrane carries the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, so more area means more ATP can be made. The fluid enclosed by the inner membrane is the matrix, where the Krebs cycle runs; it has the lower proton concentration and the higher pH. The narrow region between the two membranes holds the high proton concentration. The difference between those two regions is the gradient that drives ATP synthase. Illustrative data.
svg.text: the folds are cristae: more inner-membrane area, so more ATP synthase
Krebs cycle in the matrix; the gradient across the folded inner membrane
Protons high outside the inner membrane, low in the matrix: that difference is the gradient.
